---
title: Mixing, interventions, and results
jupyter: python3
---

A disease says *who infects whom*: `S >> I @ beta * I` reads "susceptible people become infected at a rate proportional to their contact with infected people". Everything around it is kept separate. The **routes** say who meets whom and how often; **effects** say what changes what; **interventions** say what is delivered to whom; and **results** say what comes out. Each of these is a separate object, so changing one (homogeneous mixing to a contact matrix, say, or a vaccine to a test) doesn't touch the disease.

## Routes: who meets whom

A bare state in a rate means contact with people in that state, through whatever routes the sim has. With no network, `beta * I` is the textbook `beta * I / N`, and `beta` is a transmission rate. With a network or mixing pool, the route supplies the contacts, and `beta` becomes a probability per contact (per act, on a sexual network). It is one rule: the hazard is `beta` times the contact rate times the share of contacts who are infectious, and the default contact rate is 1. Nobody has to write `/N`, a common mistake in hand-written models.

When a formula needs the number itself, it uses `I.n`, which is taken literally. This is how environmental and vector-borne transmission are written: a water reservoir or a mosquito population is just a state declared with `people=False`, and its count appears in the rate (`beta * W.n / (W.n + K)`). There is no special route type for these.

All routes are passed with `networks=`, and the disease stays the same object throughout:

```{python}
import starsim as ss
ss.options(jupyter=True)

S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
sir = ss.Disease(
    infection = S >> I @ 0.05 * I,
    recovery  = I >> R @ ss.days(10),
    init_prev = 0.01,
    name      = 'sir',
)

routes = {
    'No network':     dict(),
    'Mixing pool':    dict(networks=ss.MixingPool(n_contacts=10)),
    'Contact matrix': dict(networks=ss.contacts('Kenya'), stratify=dict(age=[0, 15, 65])),
    'Random network': dict(networks=ss.RandomNet(n_contacts=10)),
}
for label, kw in routes.items():
    sim = ss.Sim(sir, unit='day', stop=ss.days(100), verbose=0, **kw)
    sim.init()
    print(f'{label}: {sim.solver}, since {sim.solver_reason}')
```

Homogeneous mixing, a mixing pool, and a contact matrix have exact compartmental forms, so `solver='auto'` runs them as an ODE; an individual-level network doesn't, so the sim runs as agents. `auto` never approximates the mixing. Ask for `solver='ode'` on a network and Starsim uses the standard approximation (homogeneous mixing with the same mean contacts for a random network; the Anderson–May partner-change model for lasting partnerships) and prints one line saying so, or raises `CapabilityError` with `approx=False`. See [Solvers](solvers.qmd) for how the choice is made.

A list of routes is a layered population (`ss.contacts('Kenya', layer='school')`, and so on), and the force of infection sums over the layers. Space is a stratification by patch (`ss.geo.geography('Kenya', level=1)`), with an optional mobility model (`ss.geo.gravity()`, `ss.geo.radiation()`, or a matrix) that couples the patches by commuting or migration; these run under every solver. Contact tracing and the transmission log need routes that keep individual contacts, so they need agents.

## Effects: what changes what

There are two ways for one module to change another, and both are first-class:

- **`ss.modify`**, for the common case: while a condition holds, multiply (or add to, or set) a named quantity. `ss.modify(hiv.rel_trans, multiply=2.0, where=syphilis.active)` reads "for people with active syphilis, multiply HIV transmissibility by 2".
- **Ordinary Python in a module's `step()`**, for everything else: several sources and targets, boolean flags, schedules, memory.

A modifier never overwrites what it changes. Each modifiable quantity has a *base* value (what its module set) and an *effective* value (the base with every active modifier applied). Reading `sir.rel_sus[uids]` gives the base, assigning to it sets the base, and `sir.rel_sus.effective[uids]` is what transmission will use. When a modifier switches off, the quantity is simply back at its base: there is nothing to save or restore, and two modules can't clobber each other. Several modifiers on one quantity combine by one fixed rule, whatever order they were declared in: **set, then multiply, then add**.

Conditions (`where=`) use the sim's real attributes. Written before the sim exists, `ss.ppl.age > 65` is a lazy expression (an `ss.conditions.Cond`), evaluated each time it's needed. Nothing is analyzed in advance: a condition is tried on whatever the solver provides, agents or groups. `age > 65` works on groups if 65 is an age bin edge; for `age > 70` inside a bin, `auto` runs agents and an explicit `solver='ode'` stops and says why.

Because modifiers are declared, Starsim can list them all, before anything runs. Products are modifiers too, so a vaccine shows up in the same list:

```{python}
masks       = ss.modify(sir.rel_sus, multiply=0.6, where=ss.ppl.age > 65, start=ss.days(20))
vaccination = ss.vaccinate(efficacy=0.85, who=ss.ppl.age < 15, coverage=0.7, at=[ss.days(30)])
sim = ss.Sim(sir, interventions=[masks, vaccination], stratify=dict(age=[0, 15, 65]), unit='day', stop=ss.days(100), verbose=0)
sim.what_modifies(sir.rel_sus)
```

Code that writes another module's arrays directly is allowed, but isn't tracked. Nothing is accepted and then ignored: a modifier that no solver would apply raises `ss.errors.Unapplied` when the sim is built. Modules run in Starsim's ordered loop ([From model to run](build_and_run.qmd)), each seeing the current values, so mutual dependence (HIV raising syphilis susceptibility while syphilis raises HIV transmissibility) needs no special handling; any effect of the order is of order `dt`, which `sim.check_dt()` measures.

## Interventions: products and delivery

An intervention has two parts. *What* is a product (`ss.Vaccine`, `ss.Diagnostic`, `ss.Treatment`: nouns) or a change to a quantity (`ss.change`, `ss.modify`). *Delivery* is who gets it, when, and how many (`ss.vaccinate`, `ss.screen`, `ss.treat`: verbs), given by keywords (`who=`, `coverage=`, `capacity=`, `at=`, `interval=`, `at_age=`), or by one `deliver=` function when those depend on each other. Routine versus campaign delivery is a keyword, not a class. A delivery takes its product's keywords and makes the product itself (`ss.vaccinate(efficacy=0.85, ...)` makes an `ss.Vaccine`); a product is made on its own only when several deliveries give the same one.

A cascade of care is a list of ordinary deliveries, each triggered by the outcome of another:

```python
screening = ss.screen(sensitivity=0.8, specificity=0.95, coverage=0.1, interval=ss.days(7))  # a rapid test
confirm   = ss.screen(sensitivity=0.95, specificity=0.99, who=screening.positive, coverage=0.9) # a follow-up is a step of its own
treatment = ss.treat(cure=0.95, who=confirm.positive, capacity=ss.perday(50))                # while stocks last
```

An outcome such as `screening.positive` is an *event*: the people it happened to this step. Events can be joined (`a | b`), and they remember: `screening.positive.ever`, `.count`, and `.since` work anywhere a condition does. Each step runs after the steps whose events trigger it, whatever order they are listed in, so a follow-up acts on the same step as its trigger. Every delivery has results of its own (`delivered`, `eligible`, `coverage`, ...).

The same declarations run under every solver where they can. This cascade runs as an ODE, with the tests as flows thinned by sensitivity and specificity and capacity as a cap on the total flow. Some things need individuals: a test result that comes after a `delay=`, the joint of two events, `.since`, `trace=` (delivery to contacts), or a product whose effect is your own code. Under `auto` any of these makes the sim run as agents, and the reason it prints names the part.

A rule with memory ("reopen schools only after four weeks below the threshold") is a small intervention class whose `step()` keeps a flag, plus a modifier that reads it. A scenario is just a sim with its interventions; `ss.parallel({'Baseline': base, 'Masks': masks})` runs several as one `ss.MultiSim`, labeled by scenario.

## Results

Every state gets a count (`I`) and every transition a flow of the same name (`infection`), with no declaration needed. Extra results are declared with the model: a ratio (`prevalence = I / N`) or an `ss.outcome`, a weighted, delayed sum of flows for observed quantities ("half of infections are reported, five days later": `ss.outcome(0.5 * infection, delay=ss.days(5))`). An outcome moves nobody, and if the model includes testing, the tests' own `positive` results are the cases instead.

Each result knows its kind (a flow, a stock, or a ratio), and that one fact does a lot of work: resampling to weeks, or comparing with weekly data, sums a flow but reads a stock at the end of each week, and a ratio is never averaged across groups (its numerator and denominator are summed, then divided). After stratification a result is still one result with extra dimensions, so `res.I.select(age='0-14')` and `res.I.by('age')` replace names like `I_female_high`. Data attaches by column name (`data='cases.csv'` with a column called `cases`), which is also all that calibration needs (see [Randomness and fitting](randomness_and_fitting.qmd)).

A sim is one run. Many runs are an `ss.MultiSim`, whose results are the same `ss.Result` objects, each holding every run (an array with a row for each run and a column for each time point), with the scenario and any parameters swept recorded for each run. So the same methods work on one run or many: `res.select(scenario=...)`, `res.median()` and `res.quantiles()` at each time point, and `res.summarize()`, which reduces each run to one value by the result's kind (a flow to its total, a stock to its final value):

```{python}
S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
small = ss.Disease(infection=S >> I @ 0.2 * I, recovery=I >> R @ ss.days(10), init_n=dict(I=3), name='sir')
sim = ss.Sim(small, solver='gillespie', total_pop=1000, unit='day', stop=ss.days(120), verbose=0)
msim = sim.run(n_runs=20)

totals = msim.results.sir.infection.summarize() # The total infections of each run
print('Total infections in each run:', totals)
print('Share of runs with a major outbreak:', (totals > 100).mean())
```

Extinction and bimodality can't be seen in a median, which is why `msim.plot(lines=True)` draws every run, and `msim.summarize()` gives an interval as well as the median.

## Limits

- Modifiers on one quantity combine by the one rule above. Protection from several strains a person holds needs a different rule (the strongest, or a capped sum), which is `ss.immunity`; anything else is `step()` code.
- `when=` functions and `ss.modify` keep no memory apart from `hold=`; anything that must remember is a class.

The code is in `starsim/networks.py` and `solvers/mixing.py` (routes), `connectors.py` and `conditions.py` (effects), `interventions.py`, `products.py` and `solvers/deliveries.py` (interventions), and `results.py`. For the modeler's view, see the user guide on [networks](../user_guide/populations_networks.qmd), [contact matrices](../user_guide/populations_contacts.qmd), [connectors](../user_guide/interventions_connectors.qmd), [products and deliveries](../user_guide/interventions_products.qmd), [changing parameters](../user_guide/interventions_changes.qmd), [results](../user_guide/running_results.qmd), and [uncertainty and many runs](../user_guide/running_uncertainty.qmd).
